full_title: EDITHA M. BAYONA, COMPLAINANT, VS. HON. AIDA THERESITA B. BASA-DIVIVA, PRESIDING JUDGE, MUNICIPAL CIRCUIT TRIAL COURT, STA. CRUZ-CANDELARIA, ZAMBALES, RESPONDENT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)
topics: Judicial acts not subject to disciplinary action absent fraud, dishonesty, gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice
Administrative complaint is not a substitute for judicial remedies
Substantial evidence; presumption of regularity; bare allegations
Hold-departure orders are for RTCs only; first-level judges no longer conduct preliminary investigation
Arraignment without the private complainant (Rule 116, Sec. 1(f)); admonition for imprudent postponements

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Constitutional Rights > G. Liberty of Abode and Right to Travel > 2. Watchlist, Hold Departure Orders, and Precautionary Hold Departure Orders

doctrine:
**As a matter of policy, the acts of a judge in a judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action, however erroneous, as long as the judge acted in good faith. Only judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty, gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice are administratively sanctioned** (reiterating Pitney v. Judge Abrogar). Errors committed in the exercise of adjudicative functions must be corrected through judicial remedies, not administrative proceedings. Disciplinary proceedings do not complement, supplement, or substitute for judicial remedies, and an inquiry into administrative liability arising from judicial acts may be made only after the other available remedies have been settled. Bias and partiality require a showing of arbitrariness or prejudice.

**In administrative cases, the complainant bears the burden of proving the charges by substantial evidence.** Bare allegations cannot overcome the presumption that the judge regularly performed official duties. Requiring proof protects magistrates from flimsy and unsubstantiated charges.

Procedural rules reiterated and applied: (a) issuing a hold-departure order is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the RTC (OCA Circular No. 39-97), so a first-level judge who issued one "would have reeked of ignorance of the law" (Re: Occiano); (b) under A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC, first-level court judges no longer conduct preliminary investigations, which are now with the provincial or city prosecutor, and unjust vexation, a light offense, does not require one; (c) the private complainant need not be present at the arraignment unless the court requires it (Rule 116, Sec. 1(f)). A judge whose postponements were not shown to be whimsical, but who was not cautious enough in granting them, may be admonished.
facts:
On February 5, 2020, Editha M. Bayona filed a sworn complaint with the OCA charging Judge Aida Theresita B. Basa-Diviva of the MCTC of Sta. Cruz-Candelaria, Zambales, with dishonesty, violation of RA 3019, and gross ignorance of the law/procedure. Her complaint concerned three criminal cases: two against Josefina Medida-House (alarm and scandal, and violation of Section 48(3) of RA 9003), and one against Bayona herself (Criminal Case No. 5672, described as maltreatment/slight physical injuries by ill treatment). The complaint went to the JIB.

Bayona alleged the following. On September 13, 2018, the judge acted on House's handwritten, un-notarized manifestation asking permission to leave the country, which Bayona said should have complied with the rules on counter-affidavits. Bayona herself was not furnished the order setting her arraignment and was given no chance to file a counter-affidavit. The criminal complaint for unjust vexation against her had no preliminary investigation. She was arraigned on March 14, 2019 although private complainant House and her counsel were absent. The judge did not issue the warrant against House that she had warned of when House again failed to appear on July 11, 2019. Hearings were postponed many times without valid reason. She also accused the judge of bullying and harassing her, and she complained about her own counsel, Atty. Domingo A. Doctor, Jr.

The judge answered that allowing House to travel was just and lawful, and that issuing a hold-departure order was beyond an MCTC's authority. She said preliminary investigation belongs to the prosecutor under A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC, that the postponements were caused by the absence of the accused or the public prosecutor, and that the case against Bayona had in fact been dismissed. The OED-JIB recommended that the judge be fined PHP 1,000.00 for violating Section 5, Canon 6 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, that the other charges be dismissed, and that the charge against Atty. Doctor be referred to the Office of the Bar Confidant. In its March 9, 2022 Report, the JIB adopted these findings but recommended admonition instead of a fine. The judge compulsorily retired on December 28, 2021.
issues: Whether respondent judge is administratively liable for dishonesty, violation of RA 3019, or gross ignorance of the law for allowing an accused to travel abroad, for the lack of preliminary investigation, and for arraigning complainant without the private complainant.
Whether the charges of bullying, harassment, and denial of due process were proved by substantial evidence.
Whether respondent should be sanctioned for the repeated postponement of hearings.
ruling:
**1. No.** There was "no iota of evidence" of dishonesty, graft, or gross ignorance, and the complainant did not even specify the acts constituting them.

- *Travel abroad:* Allowing House to travel was an exercise of judicial function. Under Pitney v. Judge Abrogar, a judge "cannot be subjected to liability... for any of [their] official acts, no matter how erroneous, as long as [they act] in good faith." Errors in adjudication must be corrected through judicial remedies, and disciplinary proceedings do not substitute for them. **Assuming the order was erroneous, it remained judicial in nature and, absent fraud, dishonesty, or corruption, was not subject to discipline.** Issuing a hold-departure order, an act within the RTC's exclusive jurisdiction under OCA Circular No. 39-97, "would have reeked of ignorance of the law." In Re: Occiano, a first-level judge who knowingly issued one despite the circular committed "disrespect for, and a willful violation of, a lawful circular."
- *Preliminary investigation:* A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC transferred the power to conduct preliminary investigations from first-level courts to the provincial or city prosecutor, so MCTC judges are no longer authorized to conduct them. Moreover, unjust vexation, a light offense, does not require preliminary investigation.
- *Arraignment:* "[T]here is nothing irregular with the arraignment of an accused in the absence of the private complainant," who need not be present unless the court requires it.

**2. No.** The bullying, harassment, and due process charges were "bare allegations unsupported by any evidence." **The complainant bears the burden of proving her charges by substantial evidence**: relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate, enough to give reasonable ground to believe the respondent is responsible, even if not overwhelming or preponderant. This requirement protects magistrates from flimsy charges. Without proof, the presumption of regularity in the performance of official functions prevails.

**3. Admonition only.** There was no clear showing that the postponements were whimsical or capricious, and one was caused by the absence of the complainant's own witness. Considering the judge's untarnished reputation over 38 years of service, the Court agreed with the JIB that she should merely be admonished for failing to exercise more caution in granting postponements. The complaint against Atty. Doctor was referred to the Office of the Bar Confidant.
disposition: The JIB's March 9, 2022 Report and Recommendation was ADOPTED in full. The complaint for dishonesty, violation of RA 3019, and gross ignorance of the law/procedure against Judge Aida Theresita B. Basa-Diviva was DISMISSED for being judicial in nature and for lack of merit. She was ADMONISHED for failing to exercise the necessary prudence in granting postponements of scheduled hearings. The complaint against Atty. Domingo A. Doctor, Jr. was referred to the Office of the Bar Confidant for appropriate action.

bar_questions.q: Lorna is the private complainant in a slight physical injuries case pending before MTC Judge Gomez. Over Lorna's objection, Judge Gomez granted the accused's motion for permission to travel abroad for two weeks. Lorna did not move for reconsideration or file any petition. Instead she filed an administrative complaint against Judge Gomez for gross ignorance of the law and dishonesty, alleging only that the order was wrong and favored the accused. Will the administrative complaint prosper?

alac.answer: No. The complaint should be dismissed for being judicial in nature and for lack of merit.
alac.legal_basis: As a matter of policy, the acts of a judge in a judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action, no matter how erroneous, as long as the judge acted in good faith. Only judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty, gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice are administratively sanctioned. Errors in adjudication must be corrected through judicial remedies, and disciplinary proceedings do not complement, supplement, or substitute for them. The complainant must prove the charges by substantial evidence; bare allegations cannot overcome the presumption of regularity. (Bayona v. Judge Basa-Diviva, OCA-IPI No. 20-3112-MTJ, November 3, 2025, citing Pitney v. Judge Abrogar)
alac.application: Granting the accused's motion to travel was an exercise of Judge Gomez's adjudicative function. Even if the ruling was wrong, Lorna's remedy was judicial: a motion for reconsideration or the proper petition, not an administrative case. Lorna alleges only that the order was wrong and favored the accused. She offers no evidence of fraud, dishonesty, corruption, or bad faith, and partiality requires a showing of arbitrariness or prejudice. Her bare allegations cannot overcome the presumption that Judge Gomez performed her duties regularly.
alac.conclusion: The administrative complaint will be dismissed.

bar_questions.q: In a criminal case for estafa within the jurisdiction of his MCTC, Judge Tan issued a hold-departure order against the accused, on the private complainant's motion. Told that OCA Circular No. 39-97 limits hold-departure orders to cases within the exclusive jurisdiction of the RTC, Judge Tan wrote in his comment that he "firmly believed" he had authority to issue one notwithstanding the circular. May Judge Tan invoke the rule that a judge's acts in a judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action?

alac.answer: No. Judge Tan's knowing disregard of a clear circular is not a mere error of judgment, and he may be held administratively liable.
alac.legal_basis: The immunity of judicial acts from discipline does not cover errors tainted with gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice. Under OCA Circular No. 39-97, hold-departure orders may be issued only in criminal cases within the exclusive jurisdiction of the RTC; issuing one in a first-level court case "would have reeked of ignorance of the law." In Re: Occiano, cited in Bayona v. Judge Basa-Diviva (OCA-IPI No. 20-3112-MTJ, November 3, 2025), the Court held that a judge who knew the circular yet insisted he had authority committed "not just grave abuse of authority amounting to a grave misconduct or a conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service" but "disrespect for, and a willful violation of, a lawful circular of the highest court of the land."
alac.application: Unlike the judge in Bayona, who correctly refrained from issuing a hold-departure order and merely acted on a motion to travel, Judge Tan issued an order that the circular plainly reserves to RTCs. His own comment shows that he knew of the circular and chose to disregard it. That takes his act out of the protection given to good-faith judicial errors.
alac.conclusion: Judge Tan cannot hide behind the judicial-function rule; he is administratively liable for willfully violating the circular.

bar_questions.q: Accused of unjust vexation before an MCTC, Nilda complained that (a) Judge Ruiz never conducted a preliminary investigation before the case proceeded, and (b) Judge Ruiz arraigned her even though the private complainant and her counsel were absent. Nilda claims both were violations of procedure amounting to gross ignorance of the law. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No. (a) Judge Ruiz had no power to conduct a preliminary investigation, and none is required for unjust vexation. (b) Arraigning an accused without the private complainant is not irregular.
alac.legal_basis: Under A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC, the power of first-level court judges to conduct preliminary investigations was transferred to the provincial or city prosecutor, so MCTC judges are no longer authorized to conduct them. Unjust vexation, being a light offense, does not require preliminary investigation under Rule 112. Under Rule 116, Section 1(f), the private offended party need not be present at the arraignment unless the court requires it. (Bayona v. Judge Basa-Diviva, OCA-IPI No. 20-3112-MTJ, November 3, 2025)
alac.application: (a) Judge Ruiz could not have conducted a preliminary investigation even if one were required, and for a light offense like unjust vexation none is required at all. Proceeding without one is not error, much less gross ignorance. (b) The rules do not require the private complainant's presence at arraignment unless the court orders it, so arraigning Nilda in the complainant's absence was regular.
alac.conclusion: Neither act is irregular, and the charge of gross ignorance of the law must be dismissed.

notes: This Division decision was promulgated on November 3, 2025, after respondent's compulsory retirement on December 28, 2021 and before the 2025 CJCA took effect (December 21, 2025). The decision does not discuss the effect of her retirement on the case. The votes line shows Singh, J., on leave; he was designated additional member vice Marquez, J., per Raffle dated September 13, 2022. The decision is not consistent about the case against Bayona: Criminal Case No. 5672 is described as maltreatment/slight physical injuries by ill treatment, while the preliminary investigation discussion refers to an unjust vexation complaint against her. The digest follows each statement as written. The 2027 syllabus lists Rule 112 as partly repealed by A.M. No. 24-02-09-SC; check the current rules before relying on the preliminary investigation point beyond what this case holds.
